ch2_p8_concurrency_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Industrial Extraction Concurrency Workbench. Adjust concurrent workers C, network RTT, client-side render overhead, and politeness download delay. Notice how shifting from static parsing to headless SPA rendering collapses throughput from over 750 requests per second down to under 60, while memory footprint skyrockets into gigabytes.

ch2_p8_concurrency_sim_duo.text: Check out the live throughput and memory bars! With 50 workers and static parsing, we hit nearly 800 requests per second. Drag the render overhead slider to 800 milliseconds for a headless SPA: throughput plummets by 90 percent and memory explodes into gigabytes!

ch2_p8_chk1_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 1. For one million static HTML pages, Playwright processes 20 requests per second at 200 megabytes per browser, while Scrapy processes 2,000 requests per second on 50 megabytes total. If client-side JavaScript is not required, what is Scrapy's speedup ratio and memory advantage? Select your answer.

ch2_p8_chk1_duo.text: Active Checkpoint 1! Comparing 2,000 requests per second against 20 requests per second. Calculate the speedup ratio and total crawling duration, and choose Option A, B, C, or D!

ch2_p8_chk1_feedback_correct.text: Outstanding! Option B is correct. 2,000 divided by 20 is exactly 100x faster! Crawling 1,000,000 pages takes just 8.3 minutes with Scrapy versus 13.9 hours with Playwright, while consuming 40 times less RAM. Static reactors should always be preferred unless JavaScript execution is strictly mandatory.

ch2_p8_chk1_feedback_incorrect.text: Incorrect. Divide 2,000 requests per second by 20 requests per second: Scrapy is exactly 100 times faster, finishing in 8.3 minutes compared to 13.9 hours. Furthermore, achieving equivalent concurrency in Playwright requires 2,000 megabytes compared to Scrapy's 50 megabytes, a 40-fold memory savings. The correct answer is Option B.

ch2_p8_bloom_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Bloom Filter Sizing and False Positive Workbench. Use the sliders to adjust target URLs n, false positive rate p-sub-fp, and hash count k. Observe how the simulator computes the required bit array size m and optimal hash count k-star, proving how 10 million URLs can be tracked in just 11.4 megabytes of RAM.

ch2_p8_bloom_sim_duo.text: Look at the memory comparison bar! In Python sets, 10 million URLs consume 850 megabytes of RAM. But our Bloom filter bit array packs them into just 11.43 megabytes with 7 hash functions! That is a 74-fold memory reduction!

ch2_p8_chk2_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 2. A web crawler frontier tracks 10,000,000 unique visited URLs with a target false positive rate of 1.0 percent or less. What is the required RAM allocation for the Bloom filter bit array, and what is the optimal hash count k-star? Select Option A, B, C, or D.

ch2_p8_chk2_duo.text: Active Checkpoint 2! 10 million URLs with a 1 percent false positive target. Apply Burton Bloom's sizing formula to find the required megabytes of RAM and optimal hash count! Make your choice!

ch2_p8_chk2_feedback_correct.text: Spot on! Option B is correct. Using Burton Bloom's sizing formula, m equals negative n natural log of p divided by natural log of 2 squared, yielding 95.85 million bits, which is exactly 11.43 megabytes of RAM. The optimal hash count k-star equals m over n times natural log of 2, which gives exactly 7 hash functions.

ch2_p8_chk2_feedback_incorrect.text: Not quite. Let us review the arithmetic: m equals negative 10 million times natural log of 0.01 divided by 0.48045, yielding 95.85 million bits. Dividing by 8 times 1,024 times 1,024 gives 11.43 megabytes of RAM. Multiplying m over n by natural log of 2 yields k-star equals 6.64, rounded to 7 hash functions. The correct answer is Option B.
